newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will attend Palestinian meeting if invited.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will attend Palestinian meeting if invited.

text.p: The United States, in an apparent rebuff to Israel, said on Tuesday it would attend a meeting called by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on the Middle East peace deadlock if it was formally invited.

"We're aware that Chairman Arafat has called for a conference on Saturday in Gaza. We certainly, if an invitation is formally issued to the United States, will be there," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

The PLO leader wants U.S., European and Arab envoys to discuss a crisis brewing since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approved plans to build Jewish housing between Arab East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

But Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, in a hastily convened news conference, said such a meeting would violate agreements and warned that PLO efforts to bring international pressure on Israel could freeze peace moves.

"Any appeal which could bring about international involvement could -- and I am warning that such a danger exists even if Israel does not want it to come about -- bring about a freeze in the political process," Levy told reporters.
Burns said the United States would be represented at such a meeting by its consul-general in Jerusalem, Edward Abington.
"We do understand the frustration of the Palestinian leadership," Burns told a news briefing.

"They've been buffeted by some fairly significant Israeli government decisions over the last couple of weeks. Chairman Arafat obviously feels the need to talk to friendly countries around the world, and that's appropriate."
U.S. President Bill Clinton has twice criticised the Israeli housing project and Washington has also branded as ill-timed a decision by Netanyahu to close four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem.
Burns said the United States knew little about Arafat's proposed conference and planned to ask the Palestinian leadership for details.
"But we do have great respect for Chairman Arafat," he said. "If he wished to convene a group of countries, we certainly have no argument with it."

Asked about reports that Arafat had refused to accept phone calls from Netanyahu, Burns said the State Department was not aware the Palestinians had banned contacts with the Israelis and believed some contacts were under way.
"The only way something good is going to happen is if (the Palestinians) continue to talk to the Israeli government. And that's what we encourage them to do," he said.
